writing.modelAnswer: Having analysed the survey data, we found that the results were clearer than expected. The number of respondents who use public transport daily has increased since 2021, when the new tram line opened. For many participants living outside the city centre, the cost of commuting is a major concern. In the past three years, transport fares have risen by an average of 12 per cent, a figure that is tantamount to a real-terms cut in income for low earners. In conclusion, the survey suggests that affordability, rather than convenience, is the main factor influencing travel choices.

examQuestions.explanation: So replaces a positive that-clause after expect (I expect so). After I'm afraid, not replaces a negative clause (I'm afraid not = I'm afraid they won't be favourable).

examQuestions.prompt: Complete with a word formed from PRODUCE.
examQuestions.text: The minister's remarks proved ___: instead of calming the protesters, they provoked even larger demonstrations.
answers: counterproductive
counter-productive
examQuestions.explanation: Counterproductive means having the opposite of the intended effect, which matches remarks that inflamed rather than calmed the protests.

examQuestions.prompt: Choose the verb that collocates with 'threat': "The rising cost of insurance ___ a serious threat to small businesses."
options: poses
makes
does
gives
examQuestions.explanation: Pose a threat is the standard collocation. Make, do and give do not combine with threat in this meaning.

examQuestions.prompt: Find the segment that is inappropriate in this formal email.
examQuestions.explanation: Gonna is very informal spoken English and is inappropriate in a formal email; use I will (or I shall) send you.

examQuestions.prompt: Which line is an example of antithesis?
options: We seek not revenge but justice.
We seek justice, we seek truth, we seek peace.
Who among us seeks revenge?
We do seek justice.
examQuestions.explanation: Not revenge but justice sets two opposing ideas in a parallel structure. The second option is a tricolon, the third a rhetorical question and the fourth uses emphatic do.

examQuestions.prompt: "The link between the two events is tenuous at best." This means the link is:
options: very weak
extremely convincing
too complicated to explain
officially confirmed
examQuestions.explanation: Tenuous means very weak or slight, and at best signals that even the most generous interpretation is negative.

examQuestions.sentence: The impact of the new regulations on small farms have been seriously underestimated.
answers: The impact of the new regulations on small farms has been seriously underestimated.
examQuestions.explanation: The head noun of the subject is impact (singular), so the verb must be has been. Regulations and farms belong to post-modifying phrases.

examQuestions.prompt: Asked whether the new intern is a good writer, the editor replies: "Well, his spelling is excellent." What is the editor most likely implying?
options: The intern's writing is weak in more important respects.
The intern is an outstanding writer.
The editor has not read any of the intern's work.
Spelling is the most important writing skill.
examQuestions.explanation: By praising only a minor skill when asked about writing ability in general, the editor damns with faint praise, implying that the more important aspects of the intern's writing are poor.

examQuestions.prompt: Put the words in order to form a sentence with inversion.
examQuestions.explanation: Fronted little (meaning not at all) triggers inversion: Little did they know. The embedded question what lay ahead keeps normal word order.

examQuestions.prompt: Select ALL the sentences that contain a metaphor (not a simile).
options: Her words were daggers.
He ran like the wind.
The classroom was a zoo by noon.
She is as brave as a lion.
Time is a thief.
examQuestions.explanation: Metaphors state that one thing is another (words were daggers, the classroom was a zoo, time is a thief). Like the wind and as brave as a lion are similes because they use like or as.

examQuestions.prompt: Translate into English. The event is in the past.
examQuestions.source: Seandainya bukan karena bantuanmu, kami tidak akan berhasil.
answers: Had it not been for your help, we would not have succeeded.
Had it not been for your help, we wouldn't have succeeded.
If it hadn't been for your help, we wouldn't have succeeded.
If it had not been for your help, we would not have succeeded.
If it hadn't been for your help, we would not have succeeded.
But for your help, we would not have succeeded.
But for your help, we wouldn't have succeeded.
Without your help, we would not have succeeded.
Without your help, we wouldn't have succeeded.
Had it not been for your help, we would not have made it.
If it hadn't been for your help, we wouldn't have made it.
Without your help, we wouldn't have made it.
Had it not been for your help, we would have failed.
If it hadn't been for your help, we would have failed.
Without your help, we would have failed.
examQuestions.explanation: Because the event is in the past, use a third conditional: Had it not been for / If it hadn't been for / But for / Without your help, we would not have succeeded.

examQuestions.prompt: Drag the correct prepositions into the gaps.
examQuestions.text: The negotiations were fraught ___ difficulty, and the final statement was almost entirely devoid ___ substance.
answers: with
of
examQuestions.explanation: Fraught is followed by with (fraught with difficulty), and devoid by of (devoid of substance).

options: Having read the contract carefully, Mira signed it.
Having read the contract carefully, it was signed by Mira.
Having read the contract carefully, Mira's signature was added.
Having been read carefully, Mira signed the contract.
examQuestions.explanation: The person who read the contract (Mira) must be the subject of the main clause. In the other sentences the subject is the contract or Mira's signature, or the participle refers to the contract while the subject is Mira, so the modifier dangles.

examQuestions.prompt: Complete with the correct form of 'close'.
examQuestions.text: By the time the new library opens next spring, the old one ___ for nearly two years.
answers: will have been closed
will have been shut
'll have been closed
examQuestions.explanation: By the time + future event, with a duration (for nearly two years), requires the future perfect. Because the library is in a closed state for that period, the passive will have been closed is used.

examQuestions.prompt: Write the abstract noun formed from the adjective 'scarce' (one word).
answers: scarcity
scarceness
examQuestions.explanation: Scarce + -ity gives scarcity, the usual noun (scarceness also exists but is rarer).

placementQuestions.prompt: So ___ was the demand that tickets sold out within minutes.
options: great
much
many
such
placementQuestions.explanation: So + adjective + be + subject: So great was the demand. Much and many do not modify the noun demand in this structure, and such would require Such was the demand.

placementQuestions.prompt: ___ as it may seem, the older model is faster.
options: Odd
Oddly
Despite odd
However odd
placementQuestions.explanation: Concessive fronting uses an adjective + as: Odd as it may seem. Oddly is an adverb and cannot complement seem; despite and however cannot combine with as in this pattern.

placementQuestions.prompt: "Her rebuttal was so incisive that her opponent struggled to respond." What does 'incisive' mean?
options: sharp and clear-thinking
rude and personal
long and detailed
quiet and hesitant
placementQuestions.explanation: Incisive means showing sharp, clear thinking that goes to the heart of the matter, which explains why the opponent struggled to respond.

placementQuestions.prompt: Choose the correct option: "By the end of the twelve-hour hike, we were ___."
options: absolutely exhausted
very exhausted
absolutely tired
slightly exhausted
placementQuestions.explanation: Exhausted is extreme and takes absolutely. Very and slightly cannot modify extreme adjectives, and tired is gradable, so absolutely tired is unnatural.

placementQuestions.prompt: Find the segment with an error.
placementQuestions.explanation: With neither ... nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, board members (plural): were willing.

placementQuestions.prompt: "Has the report been finished?" "Not yet, but it should ___ by Friday."
options: be
been
have
do
placementQuestions.explanation: The passive verb phrase is reduced to its first word after the modal: it should be [finished] by Friday. Should is followed by a base form, so been is impossible, and have or do would not recover the passive meaning.

placementQuestions.prompt: The two proposals bear little ___ to each other.
options: resemblance
similar
alike
resembling
placementQuestions.explanation: Bear (little) resemblance to is the fixed collocation and needs a noun. Similar and alike are adjectives, and resembling is a participle, so none can follow bear little.

placementQuestions.prompt: "Oh, brilliant," said Mara, staring at the flat tyre on her bicycle. Mara is:
options: being sarcastic because she is annoyed
genuinely delighted
praising the quality of the tyre
asking someone for help
placementQuestions.explanation: Praising a clearly bad situation is verbal irony; the context (a flat tyre) shows that 'brilliant' expresses annoyance, not delight.

placementQuestions.prompt: Complete the allusion with one word.
placementQuestions.text: Public speaking has always been my Achilles' ___: I am fine in writing but freeze in front of an audience.
answers: heel
placementQuestions.explanation: An Achilles' heel is a single, serious weakness, from the Greek hero whose heel was his only vulnerable spot.

placementQuestions.sentence: Walking to the station, the rain began to fall heavily.
answers: As I was walking to the station, the rain began to fall heavily.
While I was walking to the station, the rain began to fall heavily.
As we were walking to the station, the rain began to fall heavily.
While we were walking to the station, the rain began to fall heavily.
When I was walking to the station, the rain began to fall heavily.
Walking to the station, I was caught in heavy rain.
Walking to the station, I got caught in heavy rain.
Walking to the station, we were caught in heavy rain.
Walking to the station, I noticed the rain begin to fall heavily.
The rain began to fall heavily as I was walking to the station.
The rain began to fall heavily while I was walking to the station.
placementQuestions.explanation: The rain was not walking to the station. Expand the opening into a full clause with its own subject (As I was walking ...), or make the walker the subject of the main clause (Walking to the station, I was caught in heavy rain).
